paragraphs.heading: A module with a basis
paragraphs.text: A free module is one that has a basis: a set of elements that generates the module and is linearly independent. As a direct result, each element of the module has only one set of coefficients in terms of that basis. Every vector space is free in this sense. But when the ring the coefficients come from is not a division ring (in the commutative case, not a field), some modules fail to be free.

paragraphs.heading: Building one from any set
paragraphs.text: Take any set S and any ring R, and there is a free R-module whose basis is S. It is known as the free module on S; another name is the module of formal R-linear combinations from S. An element is a formal linear combination of members of the set, in which only finitely many coefficients are nonzero. Any R-linear map out of this module is fixed completely by what it does on the set itself, so a map given on the set can be extended by linearity.

paragraphs.heading: Rank
paragraphs.text: If R has invariant basis number, any two bases of a free R-module have the same size; nonzero commutative rings are examples of such rings. The size of a basis is then called the rank of the free module. When that size is a finite number n, the module is said to be free of rank n. For any non-negative integer n, Rⁿ, made of n copies of R, is free, and its rank is n when R has invariant basis number.

paragraphs.heading: Examples
paragraphs.text: A ring R is itself a free module of rank one, and any unit element works as a basis. When R is commutative, the polynomial ring R[X] is free, with 1, X, X², ... as one possible basis. A free abelian group is exactly a free module over the integers Z. Over a principal ideal domain such as Z, each submodule of a free module is again free.

paragraphs.heading: Sums and products
paragraphs.text: A direct sum of free modules is free. In fact, every free left module over R is, up to isomorphism, a direct sum of copies of R. An infinite cartesian product of free modules, on the other hand, is generally not free.

paragraphs.heading: Wider families
paragraphs.text: Many facts about free modules carry over to larger classes. Projective modules are the direct summands of free modules, and Kaplansky's theorem says a projective module over a local ring is free. Flat modules are those for which tensoring with them preserves exact sequences. Torsion-free modules form a broader class still. For a module over a PID such as Z that is finitely generated, being free, projective, flat and torsion-free all come to the same thing.

paragraphs.heading: Sometimes undecidable
paragraphs.text: Whether a module is free can even be undecidable in the sense of set theory. A famous case is the Whitehead problem: is a Whitehead group free? That problem turned out to be independent of ZFC.
